name: Frontalis sling ptosis surgery

lead: Frontalis sling surgery treats a drooping upper eyelid (ptosis) by connecting the lid's tarsal plate to the frontalis muscle of the forehead. After the procedure, raising the brow also raises the eyelid, which opens the eye and can correct lid asymmetry.

It is mostly used when the lid's own lifting muscle, the levator, is weak, for example in congenital ptosis. Meta-analyses and a Cochrane review compare techniques and sling materials, and appearance-related outcomes are tracked alongside function.

paras: A surgeon places a sling made from silicone rod, suture, or the patient's own fascia between the lid and the brow and adjusts the lid height. Techniques include Fox pentagon and Crawford-type patterns, and open or closed approaches. Surgeons choose by levator function and patient factors.
Reported problems include undercorrection, overcorrection, recurrence, exposure of the cornea or dry eye when the eye cannot fully close, and asymmetry. Recurrence rates differ by sling material.

chain: Sling links lid to forehead muscle
More open eyes and better lid symmetry
angle.text: The lid is mechanically coupled to the brow, so lifting the brow opens the eye. It is chosen when the lid muscle cannot do this work itself, giving a more open eye and often a more symmetrical look.

lead: Frontalis sling surgery, also called frontalis suspension, is an operation for ptosis, in which the tarsal plate of the upper eyelid is coupled to the frontalis muscle so that movement of the brow and forehead moves the lid [1][2]. It is used when levator function is poor, because the standard levator-based repairs are less likely to be effective [1].

Appearance is part of its goal: it raises a drooping lid, opens the eye and can narrow differences between the two sides. In people with severe congenital ptosis, treatment is also aimed at vision, since untreated ptosis can lead to amblyopia and astigmatism [3][4].
Randomised and comparative research examines the sling's materials, patterns and alternatives such as levator resection and frontalis flap [2][5][6].

paras: The sling couples the tarsal plate to the frontalis muscle so brow movement moves the lid [2]. In severe congenital ptosis, defined in one review as levator function of 4 mm or less, the evaluated techniques included frontalis flap, frontalis suspension and maximal levator resection [4].

Materials include silicone rods, polytetrafluoroethylene or polybutylate-coated polyester sutures, and autologous fascia lata [2][6]. Comparisons of Fox pentagon and single-triangle patterns, and of open versus closed silicone rod techniques, have been studied in randomised trials [7][8][9].

A meta-analysis of flap, silicone rod and autologous fascial techniques found no significant difference in under- or overcorrection or total complications, and recurrence was higher with silicone (7%) than with flap [3]. The American Academy of Ophthalmology review notes variable definitions of success, revision surgery and exposure keratopathy [4].

A meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (909 eyes, 657 patients) found the frontalis sling gave a significantly higher margin reflex distance than levator plication, while levator resection gave greater palpebral fissure height [5]. A Cochrane review addressed sling materials [2], and a randomised comparison of frontalis suspension with levator resection examined eyelid function in poor levator function [6]. Randomised trials also compared Fox pentagon and single-triangle patterns [7].
